== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not assessable: Engagement spanned 2019-2021 across ideation, consultation, and MoA signing, but no information is reported on non-participation or drop-out among consulted local governments, sarpanches, or post-MoA participating gram panchayats.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): Single-district participatory pilot with no comparator group and multiple concurrent institutional drivers, including prior donor-supported urban FSM capacity (Project Nirmal), SBM Phase 2 (2020-2025), the Odisha Rural Sanitation Policy (2020), and post-MoA IEC campaigns (PDF pp. 3, 5).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong to adequate: Accurately specifies the constitutional, policy, and contractual framework—including the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (Schedules XI and XII, Article 243ZD DPCs), DDWS letter S-18011/6/2021-SBM-DDWS (14 September 2021), Odisha Rural Sanitation Policy 2020, and the 28 December 2020 Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) across 17 gram panchayats—and critically distinguishes a non-binding MoA from an enforceable contract (PDF pp. 2-3, 6, 10, 12).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Qualitative data collection (consultations, structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, direct and indirect observations) lacks reported interview schedules, observation protocols, or coding procedures, and embedded advisor-implementers report no reflexivity safeguards (PDF pp. 3-4).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Pre-pilot baseline FSTP capacity (27 kLD, ~50% utilization, 13% rural share in Jan 2019-Feb 2020) is documented from municipal operational logs (PDF p. 8) and a 50% relative reduction in the rural distance surcharge is noted (PDF p. 10), but post-MoA claims of increased rural sanitation access (PDF p. 1) are presented without any post-December 2020 service-volume, tariff-level, or household-uptake data.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: Asymmetric reporting between baseline operational figures and post-intervention outcomes; the Abstract states that the partnership increased rural access to sanitation services within a short period (PDF p. 1), yet Results present zero post-MoA service delivery statistics, exact rupee tariffs, or verbatim stakeholder interview data.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Dhenkanal was purposively selected because it already possessed a donor-supported operational FSTP under Project Nirmal where the authors' organization served as knowledge partner (PDF p. 5), and sampling/selection criteria for the 8 interviewed sarpanches (out of 212 gram panchayats) and consultation participants are unreported (PDF p. 3).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly state their research question—examining what Dhenkanal's pilot experiment reveals about the challenges and opportunities for delivering sanitation services through local-level intergovernmental urban-rural partnerships in India—and situate its importance relative to SBM Phase 2 mainstreaming in September 2021.

Qualitative practice research combining stakeholder consultations, interviews, institutional observation, and documentary analysis of the partnership agreement is appropriate for investigating governance processes, accountability structures, spatial planning dilemmas, and intergovernmental negotiation dynamics in a novel institutional pilot.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF p. 3); Section 2.1 Methods and Materials (PDF pp. 3-4)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: A longitudinal practice-research case study (2019-2021) of an early-moving district with an existing FSTP, paired with theoretical framing from international intermunicipal cooperation literature, appropriately addresses the exploratory institutional question, and the authors acknowledge the scope limits of a retrospective single-system case.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1-2.2 (PDF pp. 3-5); Section 5.1 (PDF p. 12); Section 6 (PDF pp. 13-14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Although site selection of Dhenkanal district is clearly justified (PDF p. 5), the paper does not explain how the 8 sarpanches interviewed in 2020 were chosen from among 212 gram panchayats, which threshold rule ultimately selected the 17 signatory gram panchayats within the 10 km analysis, or which specific officials participated in consultations.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Data sources are listed broadly (stakeholder consultations, structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, direct and indirect observations during 2019-2021, FSTP operational logs for 2019-2020, geospatial/Census data, and a 2020 survey of 1000 rural households reported in prior grey literature [13,14]), but no interview protocols, field-note procedures, consultation counts/durations, or post-MoA monitoring methods are described.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1, Figures 2-3 (PDF pp. 3-4); Section 4.1, Figure 6 (PDF p. 8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors and their institution (Centre for Policy Research, supported by BMGF) served as knowledge partner for Project Nirmal and actively co-designed, facilitated, and helped implement the urban-rural partnership pilot with district and local governments. Despite this embedded action-research role—and noting on PDF p. 12 that negotiation proceeded with partnership formalization as a foregone conclusion—the paper includes no reflexivity analysis of how researcher involvement and donor backing shaped local decisions or evaluative judgments.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 2.1-2.2 (PDF pp. 3-5); Section 5.3 (PDF p. 12); Funding & Acknowledgments (PDF p. 14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The back matter states that informed consent was obtained from all participants, but declares Institutional Review Board review 'Not applicable' without justification despite primary household surveys and structured interviews with local leaders, and provides no discussion of confidentiality or power asymmetries in government-facilitated consultations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Institutional Review Board Statement & Informed Consent Statement (PDF p. 14)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: Aside from noting that insights cluster around planning, responsibility/accountability, and financing (PDF p. 4), no qualitative coding framework, thematic analysis process, triangulation method, or primary interview evidence is reported, and causal/evaluative claims in the Abstract (such as increased short-term rural access to sanitation services) are not substantiated with post-MoA empirical data in the Results.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 2.1, Figure 3 (PDF p. 4); Sections 4-5 (PDF pp. 7-13)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Institutional findings are clearly structured across three thematic pillars—planning (FSTP spare capacity vs. non-contiguous gram panchayat boundaries), responsibility and accountability (weaknesses of a non-binding MoA and broken political accountability chains), and financing (50% reduction in rural distance surcharge, unrecovered capital costs, and rate-rebasing needs)—with explicit discussion of scope boundaries, though post-MoA access claims lack presented empirical verification.

Valuable exploratory practice-based contribution: documents one of India's earliest local intergovernmental urban-rural FSM partnerships (December 2020 MoA) ahead of national SBM 2.0 mainstreaming, surfacing concrete legal-institutional lessons on fragmented village geography, non-enforceable MoAs versus contracts, and rural surcharge equity, though methodological opacity and missing post-intervention outcome metrics limit empirical strength.
domain_ratings.rating: Valuable exploratory contribution with notable methodological limitations
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF pp. 2-3); Section 5 (PDF pp. 11-13); Section 6 (PDF pp. 13-14)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: S081 (Dasgupta & Agarwal, 2022) is a primary qualitative participatory practice-research (action-research) case study examining an experimental urban-rural local government partnership for faecal sludge management (FSM) in Dhenkanal district, Odisha, India (2019-2021), where Dhenkanal Municipality and 17 neighbouring gram panchayats signed a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) on 28 December 2020. Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits moderate to high methodological concern (4 Yes, 3 Can't tell, and 2 No items across Q1-Q9). Its strengths lie in its clear research aims (Q1), appropriate qualitative practice-research framing (Q2, Q3), and lucid institutional analysis of India's constitutional decentralization architecture, spatial boundary mismatches across non-contiguous gram panchayats, accountability deficits in non-binding intergovernmental MoAs, and tariff surcharge equity (Q9, Q10). However, methodological rigor is substantially weakened by unreported recruitment/selection procedures for the 8 interviewed sarpanches and consultation participants (Q4), undocumented data collection protocols (Q5), absence of IRB review justification (Q7), lack of a transparent qualitative analytic/coding procedure (Q8), absence of researcher reflexivity despite the authors' embedded role as BMGF-funded technical advisors co-designing the pilot (Q6), and unsubstantiated Abstract claims of increased rural service access without post-MoA empirical uptake data.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate to high methodological concern (2 No and 3 Can't tell items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Qualitative participatory practice-research (action-research) single-district field case study drawing on stakeholder consultations, structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, direct/indirect observations, MoA documentary analysis, and descriptive baseline FSTP operational records
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 1-3); Section 2.1 Methods and Materials & Figures 2-3 (PDF pp. 3-4); Section 2.2 Site of Enquiry (PDF pp. 4-5); Section 3 Overview of Key Concepts (PDF pp. 5-7); Section 4 Results (PDF pp. 7-11); Section 5 Discussion (PDF pp. 11-13); Section 6 Conclusions (PDF pp. 13-14); Back matter statements on Funding, IRB, and Informed Consent (PDF p. 14).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper is a primary qualitative practice-research field case study ('As part of our practice research, we supported the district government pilot the approach. The data, consultations, and observations underpinning the experiment form the basis of our insights', PDF p. 1; Section 2.1, PDF pp. 3-4), directly matching the CASP Qualitative Checklist (which covers qualitative documentary/field and participatory case studies, including researcher-participant reflexivity in Q6). MMAT was not selected because the 2020 survey of 1000 rural households and the 10 km spare-capacity model are reported in separate publications ([13,14,31]) rather than as a primary quantitative empirical component with sampling/statistical methods in this paper, and only descriptive pre-pilot FSTP operational figures (2019-2020) are cited for planning context. ROBINS-I does not apply because there is no comparator arm or quantitative pre-post intervention effect estimation.
